name: Medical Devices & Medtech
one_liner: Medtech companies design and sell devices, implants, diagnostics and equipment to providers, with economics shaped by clinical evidence, hospital purchasing and reimbursement.
how_it_makes_money: Revenue comes from selling capital equipment, implants and single-use devices to hospitals and clinics, often with recurring consumables, service contracts and razor-and-blade models. Adoption depends on regulatory clearance, reimbursement codes, surgeon preference and group purchasing contracts.
revenue_formula: Revenue = procedures × device utilization per procedure × average selling price
Capital + consumables revenue = installed base × procedures per system × consumable revenue per procedure + new system sales
cost_structure: Cost of goods sold: materials and precision manufacturing
Sales and marketing: large field sales forces and clinical specialists
R&D: typically high single digits to low teens as a share of revenue
Regulatory and quality: FDA submissions, clinical trials, quality systems
Distribution and inventory: consigned inventory and loaner kits at hospitals
margins: Established device makers often earn gross margins of roughly 60-70% and solid operating margins; differentiated innovators do better than commoditized categories exposed to hospital price pressure.

key_metrics.name: Procedure volume
key_metrics.what: Number of relevant surgeries or tests; the underlying demand driver.

key_metrics.name: Average selling price (ASP)
key_metrics.what: Price per device; tracks pricing power against hospital purchasing pressure.

key_metrics.name: Installed base and utilization
key_metrics.what: Systems in the field and how intensively they are used; drives recurring revenue.

key_metrics.name: Recurring revenue share
key_metrics.what: Portion from consumables and service; makes revenue more predictable.

key_metrics.name: Organic growth
key_metrics.what: Growth excluding acquisitions and currency; shows underlying demand.

key_metrics.name: Gross margin
key_metrics.what: Revenue minus product costs; reflects differentiation and manufacturing scale.

trends: Robotic surgery expanding into more procedures and competitors
Procedures moving to ambulatory surgery centers, changing buyers and price points
Portfolio reshaping through spin-offs and tuck-in acquisitions
Remote monitoring, wearables and AI-enabled diagnostics
Tariffs and supply chain resilience affecting cost and sourcing
Tighter hospital capital budgets lengthening equipment sales cycles
